questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Renewable and non-renewable classification
questions.learningObjective: Classify resources as renewable or non-renewable
questions.stem: Student 01 classifies solar energy and coal in a study group revision.

options.text: Solar energy is renewable; coal is non-renewable.
Both are renewable resources.
Both are non-renewable resources.
Coal is renewable; solar is non-renewable.

questions.explanation: Solar energy is replenished continuously, while coal forms over geological time. Classifying both the same way is wrong.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Stock resources and flow resources
questions.stem: Student 02 distinguishes stock and flow resources during revision.

options.text: Stocks are continuously replenished; flows are finite.
Stocks are finite; flows are continuously replenished.
Both stocks and flows are finite.
Both stocks and flows are unlimited.

questions.explanation: Stock resources are finite accumulations, while flow resources are continuously replenished. Swapping or ignoring either property is wrong.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: The reserve-to-resource ratio
questions.stem: Student 03 explains the reserve-to-resource ratio in a study group.

options.text: It compares renewable to non-renewable resources.
It compares total resources to annual consumption.
It compares economically recoverable reserves to total resources.
It compares exports to imports of minerals.

questions.explanation: The reserve-to-resource ratio compares economically recoverable reserves with total estimated resources. It is not about consumption, classification, or trade.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: The two channels of a resource curse
questions.learningObjective: State the two channels of a resource curse
questions.stem: Student 04 lists the two channels of a resource curse.

options.text: Trade surplus and budget surplus.
Inflation and deflation only.
Population growth and urbanisation.
Dutch disease and institutional weakening.

questions.explanation: The resource curse operates through Dutch disease and institutional weakening. Price or demographic changes alone are not the channels.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Reading a cost table for where mineral rent lies
questions.learningObjective: Locate mineral rent in a cost table
questions.stem: Student 05 reads a cost table to find where mineral rent lies.

options.text: Rent is the total revenue from sales.
Rent is the surplus after all costs are deducted from price.
Rent is the fixed cost of extraction.
Rent is the transport charge only.

questions.explanation: Mineral rent is the surplus remaining after all costs are deducted from price. Revenue, costs, or transport alone are not rent.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Mineral rent per tonne
questions.stem: Student 06 computes mineral rent per tonne from a price and cost table.

options.text: Rent per tonne is total cost per tonne only.
Rent per tonne is price plus total cost per tonne.
Rent per tonne is price minus total cost per tonne.
Rent per tonne is price times total cost.

questions.explanation: Rent per tonne equals price minus total cost per tonne. Adding, using cost alone, or multiplying gives wrong rent.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Leakage from an enclave economy
questions.learningObjective: Explain leakage from an enclave economy
questions.stem: Student 07 explains leakage from an enclave economy.

options.text: Leakage increases local employment.
All revenue stays in the local economy.
Leakage is only about tax evasion.
Profits and wages leave the local economy.

questions.explanation: In an enclave economy, profits and wages often flow out, limiting local benefit. Assuming all revenue stays local is wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Land-use change under an agribusiness contract
questions.learningObjective: Describe land-use change under a contract
questions.stem: Student 08 describes land-use change under an agribusiness contract.

options.text: Land becomes more diversified automatically.
Smallholder land shifts to large-scale monoculture.
Land reverts to forest without input.
No land-use change occurs.

questions.explanation: Agribusiness contracts often convert smallholder land to large-scale monoculture. Assuming diversification or no change is wrong.

questions.topic: How a plantation organises its labour

options.text: It uses wage labour under central management.
It relies only on family labour.
It uses no labour at all.

questions.explanation: Plantations typically use wage labour managed centrally. Family labour alone is more typical of smallholdings.

options.text: Low input systems use more energy.
All food systems use equal energy.
High input systems use more energy per hectare.
Energy input is irrelevant to classification.

questions.explanation: Food systems can be classified by energy input per unit area. High-input systems use more energy, not equal or less.

questions.topic: Concession royalty on gross output value

options.text: The royalty is 1005.
The royalty is 5.
The royalty is 500.
The royalty is 50.

questions.explanation: Five percent of 1000 is 50. Using the wrong percentage or adding gives wrong royalties.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Capturing mineral rent without damaging the wider economy
questions.stem: Student 12 asks how to capture mineral rent without damaging the wider economy.

options.text: Tax all revenue at a high flat rate.
Use a rent tax that does not distort investment.
Ban all mineral exports.
Ignore rent and rely on volume.

questions.explanation: A rent tax targets surplus without distorting investment or production decisions. High taxes, bans, or ignoring rent are worse.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Risk profile of a subsistence crop
questions.learningObjective: Describe risk profile of a subsistence crop
questions.stem: Student 13 describes the risk profile of a subsistence crop.

options.text: No risk at all.
High market risk and low weather risk.
Low market risk but high weather risk.
Only financial risk matters.

questions.explanation: Subsistence crops face weather risk but little market risk because they are not sold. Reversing or ignoring risks is wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A cash crop and the volatility it exposes
questions.learningObjective: Describe volatility from a cash crop
questions.stem: Student 14 describes the volatility a cash crop exposes.

options.text: Volatility is always beneficial.
Cash crops remove all income volatility.
Only weather causes volatility.
Price swings in global markets create income volatility.

questions.explanation: Cash crops expose farmers to global price swings, creating income volatility. Claiming stability or weather-only risk is wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Labour displaced by mechanised harvesting
questions.stem: Student 15 explains labour displaced by mechanised harvesting.

options.text: Mechanisation increases labour demand.
Machines replace manual workers and reduce jobs.
No workers are displaced.
Only skilled workers are displaced.

questions.explanation: Mechanised harvesting replaces manual labour and reduces jobs. Claiming increased demand or no displacement is wrong.

questions.topic: The input dependency of a green revolution package

questions.stem: Student 16 explains the input dependency of a green revolution package.

options.text: Only labour is required.
Green revolution needs no external inputs.
High yields require purchased seeds, fertiliser, and water.
Inputs reduce yields.

questions.explanation: Green revolution packages depend on purchased seeds, fertiliser, and water to achieve high yields. Denying inputs or their role is wrong.

questions.stem: Student 17 relates tenure security to input use.

options.text: Only rented land receives inputs.
Tenure security reduces input use.
Tenure has no effect on inputs.
Secure tenure encourages more input investment.

questions.explanation: Secure tenure gives farmers confidence to invest in inputs. Insecure tenure discourages such investment.

questions.topic: What registered title changes about farm investment
questions.learningObjective: Explain registered title effect on investment
questions.stem: Student 18 explains what registered title changes about farm investment.

options.text: It has no effect on investment.
It enables collateral and long-term investment.
It reduces investment incentives.
It only affects tax payments.

questions.explanation: Registered title provides security that enables collateral and long-term investment. Denying or reversing this is wrong.

questions.topic: The price effect of an agricultural cooperative
questions.stem: Student 19 explains the price effect of an agricultural cooperative.

options.text: Cooperatives have no price effect.
Cooperatives lower prices for farmers.
Bulk selling improves bargaining power and prices.
Only middlemen set prices.

questions.explanation: Cooperatives improve bargaining power through bulk selling, raising prices for members. Claiming lower or no effect is wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Collateral in rural credit
questions.stem: Student 20 explains collateral in rural credit.

options.text: Collateral reduces loan size.
No collateral is needed for rural loans.
Only cash is accepted as collateral.
Land title often serves as collateral for loans.

questions.explanation: Land title commonly serves as collateral in rural credit. Denying collateral or restricting it to cash is wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: The yield gap and its two components
questions.stem: Student 21 explains the yield gap and its two components.

answer.exemplar: The yield gap is the difference between potential and actual yield, split into an efficiency gap from management and a resource gap from inputs.

questions.explanation: The gap has an efficiency component from management and a resource component from inputs. Ignoring either gives an incomplete view.

questions.topic: Stages in establishing a village land bank
questions.stem: Student 22 explains stages in establishing a village land bank.

answer.exemplar: A village land bank is established by identifying land, registering rights, pooling resources, and allocating plots under agreed rules.

questions.explanation: The stages include identifying land, registering rights, pooling resources, and allocating plots. Skipping stages breaks the process.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a fertiliser subsidy does to the water
questions.stem: Student 23 explains what a fertiliser subsidy does to the water.

answer.exemplar: A fertiliser subsidy can increase application rates, raising nutrient runoff and degrading water quality through eutrophication.

questions.explanation: Subsidies may increase fertiliser use and runoff, harming water. Ignoring this effect is wrong.

questions.topic: Attributing a yield gap to inputs
questions.learningObjective: Explain attributing yield gap to inputs
questions.stem: Student 24 explains attributing a yield gap to inputs.

answer.exemplar: Attributing a yield gap to inputs requires comparing actual input levels with recommended levels and linking shortfalls to yield losses.

questions.explanation: The attribution links input shortfalls to yield losses. Ignoring input levels gives weak attribution.

questions.topic: Genetic uniformity and disease susceptibility
questions.stem: Student 25 explains genetic uniformity and disease susceptibility.

answer.exemplar: Genetic uniformity in crops reduces diversity, making large areas vulnerable to the same disease and causing widespread losses.

questions.explanation: Uniform genetics increase disease susceptibility across large areas. Diversity would reduce this risk.

questions.topic: Fertiliser lost to drainage
questions.stem: Student 26 explains fertiliser lost to drainage.

answer.exemplar: Fertiliser lost to drainage occurs when nutrients leach below the root zone, reducing efficiency and polluting groundwater.

questions.explanation: Drainage can leach nutrients below roots, wasting fertiliser and polluting water. This reduces efficiency.

questions.stem: Student 27 explains the nutritional service of a legume in a rotation.

answer.exemplar: A legume in rotation fixes atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility and reducing the need for synthetic fertiliser.

questions.explanation: Legumes fix nitrogen, boosting soil fertility and cutting fertiliser needs. Ignoring this service undervalues rotations.

questions.stem: Student 28 explains how integrated pest management cuts inputs.

questions.explanation: IPM uses multiple control methods to reduce chemical inputs. Relying only on chemicals misses the benefit.

questions.stem: Student 29 explains pastoral movement as a drought response.

answer.exemplar: Pastoralists move livestock to follow available forage and water, reducing drought risk and preventing overgrazing in one area.

questions.explanation: Movement spreads grazing pressure and follows resources, mitigating drought. Staying fixed worsens degradation.

answer.exemplar: A rising water table brings salts to the surface, where evaporation concentrates them and degrades soil productivity.

questions.explanation: Rising water tables deposit salts that accumulate on the surface. This degrades soil and reduces yields.

questions.topic: A cash crop and the volatility it exposes
questions.stem: Student 54 first describes volatility, then explains it.

options.text: Only weather causes volatility.
Cash crops remove all income volatility.
Price swings in global markets create income volatility.
Volatility is always beneficial.

questions.explanation: Cash crops expose farmers to global price swings, creating income volatility. Claiming stability or weather-only risk is wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Labour displaced by mechanised harvesting
questions.stem: Student 55 first explains displacement, then applies it.

options.text: Only skilled workers are displaced.
Mechanisation increases labour demand.
No workers are displaced.
Machines replace manual workers and reduce jobs.

questions.explanation: Mechanised harvesting replaces manual labour and reduces jobs. Claiming increased demand or no displacement is wrong.

questions.topic: The input dependency of a green revolution package
questions.stem: Student 56 first explains dependency, then applies it.

options.text: Green revolution needs no external inputs.
High yields require purchased seeds, fertiliser, and water.

Inputs reduce yields.

questions.explanation: Green revolution packages depend on purchased seeds, fertiliser, and water to achieve high yields. Denying inputs or their role is wrong.

questions.topic: Reading tenure security against input use
questions.stem: Student 57 first relates tenure to inputs, then applies it.

options.text: Tenure has no effect on inputs.
Tenure security reduces input use.
Secure tenure encourages more input investment.
Only rented land receives inputs.

questions.explanation: Secure tenure gives farmers confidence to invest in inputs. Insecure tenure discourages such investment.

questions.topic: The price effect of an agricultural cooperative
questions.stem: Student 59 first explains cooperative pricing, then applies it.
